query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-pressure hot isostatic pressing (HIP) treatment at an intermediate temperature (close to but below the melting point of Cu) will promote transient liquid-phase sintering of the Cu matrix, enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding, and suppress both phase separation and void formation, thereby improving the thermal conductivity of the composite under high thermal flux and irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite with discrete or interconnected tungsten features in a copper matrix that exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
generation.intervention: A single HIP treatment at a controlled intermediate temperature (e.g., around 800–900°C) under high pressure for a short duration.
generation.conditions: Processing during HIP treatment tuned to leverage transient diffusion without melting Cu, and service conditions typical of plasma-facing material joints (elevated heat flux and irradiation environments).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding achieved by facilitating a transient liquid phase in the Cu matrix, which heals voids and limits the coalescence of Cu-rich regions.
generation.mechanism: Under high pressure and at an optimized temperature, the Cu phase becomes sufficiently mobile to wet the tungsten ligaments, improving atomic diffusion at the interface. This bonding reduces the interfacial energy, thereby kinetically hindering the phase separation and void coalescence that normally degrade thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HIP-treated composite will exhibit a more homogeneous microstructure with sealed interfaces, leading to higher effective thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite when subjected to heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite, which shows pronounced phase separation and interfacial void formation that compromise its thermal conductivity under service conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective within a specific window of treatment parameters (temperature, pressure, and duration) and may not work if the Cu matrix becomes over-molten or if the pressure is insufficient to drive proper interfacial diffusion; its efficacy under long-term irradiation remains to be confirmed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal HIP processing conditions (temperature, pressure, and duration) need precise determination, and the stability of the improved microstructure under prolonged irradiation and cyclic thermal stresses is still uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical W–Cu composite samples. Subject one set to HIP treatment under the proposed conditions and leave the other set untreated. Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM with EDS) before and after subjecting both sets to accelerated heat-transfer and irradiation tests. Measure the thermal conductivity of both sets using techniques such as laser flash analysis.
measurements: Quantitative microstructural assessment of interfacial voids and phase homogeneity (via SEM/TEM)
Thermal conductivity values before and after simulated service conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HIP-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity and thermal conductivity, or if they develop similar or worse phase separation/void formation relative to untreated samples after heat and irradiation testing, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

The influence of composition and cooling rate on the microstructural development and properties of (CoCrCuTi)100−xFex (x = 0, 5, 10, 12.5, 15) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) were investigated utilizing arc-melting and EM levitation-melting, followed by quenching against a copper substrate or chill mold. Arc-melted samples with no iron addition revealed BCC1 + BCC2 phases, followed by an interdendritic FCC Cu-rich phase. However, with the addition of 5 to 15% Fe, a Cu-lean C14 Laves phase emerged, accompanied by an interdendritic Cu-rich FCC phase. At 10 at. % Fe, lower cooling rates (1–75 K/s) resulted in LPS, leading to the formation of Cu-lean L1 and Cu-rich L2 liquid phases. Increasing the cooling rate to ~400–700 K/s, the microstructure transformed into Cu-lean dendrites, with an interdendritic Cu-rich phase. However, coarse dendrites developed with a DAS of ~0.6–0.8 μm, surrounded by the Cu-rich liquid that was rejected and solidified at the end. At ~1000–1600 K/s, fine dendrites formed with a DAS of ~0.4–0.5 μm, alongside an interdendritic Cu-rich phase. Alloys with 12.5 to 15 at. % Fe developed LPS regardless of cooling rate.
